examples.explain: Merged: [1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 9, 11, 12]. The middle two are 4 and 7.

followUp: The same partition idea finds the k-th smallest value of two sorted arrays. What changes?
hints: Merging works in O(m + n). To beat it, describe the median without building the merged array.
The median splits all values into a left half and a right half. If i values of the left half come from nums1, how many come from nums2?
Binary-search i over the shorter array. The split is right when nums1[i−1] ≤ nums2[j] and nums2[j−1] ≤ nums1[i].

insight.mnemonic: Cut both decks so every card on the left is ≤ every card on the right.
insight.oneLiner: Don't merge - choose how many of the left half come from the shorter array, and binary-search that count.

recall.a: j = half − i must stay within 0..n for every i in 0..m. That holds when m ≤ n, and it makes the search O(log(min(m, n))).
nums1[i−1] ≤ nums2[j] and nums2[j−1] ≤ nums1[i] - the within-array pairs are sorted already.
recall.q: What two comparisons decide whether a split is correct?

recall.a: Treat the missing neighbours as −∞ (left) and +∞ (right), so the comparisons still work.
recall.q: How do you handle i = 0 or i = m?

signals: two sorted arrays, a k-th element or median
O(log) required on more than one array
insight.why: A left half of fixed size half = (m + n + 1) / 2 is fully described by i, the number taken from nums1. If nums1's last-left is too big, i is too large; if nums2's last-left is too big, i is too small. That's a sorted yes/no question over 0..m, so it takes O(log m) probes.

oneLiner: Don't merge - choose how many of the left half come from the shorter array, and binary-search that count.

pitfalls.explain: With an even count the median is the average of two values, which can end in .5. Use / 2, not // 2.
pitfalls.title: Used integer division for the even case

pitfalls.explain: When the total count is even there are two middle values. The median is their average.
pitfalls.title: Returned one middle value instead of their average

pitfalls.explain: When i is 0 or m (or j is 0 or n), one neighbour of the cut doesn't exist. Use −∞ and +∞ for the missing values instead of indexing.
pitfalls.title: Read past the end of an array

solutions.idea: Walk both arrays like the merge step of merge sort, stopping at the middle and keeping the last two values. Simple and correct, but linear.
solutions.name: Merge to the middle

footnotes.text: Don't merge - choose. The left half takes some count i from nums1 and the rest, j = half - i, from nums2. Only i is free, and it ranges over 0..m, so binary-search it.
Missing neighbours become -inf and +inf, so taking none (or all) of an array needs no special case: an empty side can't break the ordering check.
Each array is sorted on its own, so only the two cross pairs need checking: nums1's last-left against nums2's first-right, and vice versa.

solutions.idea: Pick i values from the shorter array and half − i from the other. Compare the values beside the cut: the comparison says whether i is too big or too small, so binary search finds the median split.
solutions.name: Binary-search the partition

starter:
class Solution:
    def findMedianSortedArrays(self, nums1: List[int], nums2: List[int]) -> float:
statement:
You're given two arrays `nums1` and `nums2`, each sorted in non-decreasing order (either may be empty, but not both). Return the **median** of all their values combined: the middle value of the merged order, or the average of the two middle values when the total count is even.

Aim for **O(log(m + n))** time, where `m` and `n` are the two lengths - without merging the arrays.
title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
